# Simorgh: architecture evaluation and re-architecture proposal

*Generated by Claude Code using Claude Fable 5.1 on 2026-09-18, against `main` at commit `38a9049`.*

This document answers two questions the creator asked on the same evening:

1. **Review and evaluate the architecture. Where did I go wrong, and how do I improve it?**
2. **As an AI-agent scientist: where did we go right, and how should Sim be re-architected so it is aligned with where agents are going, keeps compounding in capability, reasons better, runs long tasks, interacts better with its environment and its people, and can keep growing toward something much more general?**

Part I (sections 1 to 6) is the evaluation. Part II (sections 7 to 12) is the forward design. Section 13 is the findings catalogue with evidence. Section 14 records the method and its limits.

---

## 1. Executive summary

Simorgh is a serious piece of work. Eighteen packages, 87k lines of Python, 856 commits in fifteen days, and a set of architectural commitments that most agent projects never make: a single shared dependency, a structurally enforced approval gate on every effect, an append-only event log as the only state, worktree-isolated self-modification with a test-gated bootloader that can roll itself back. Those commitments are real in the code, not just in the documents, and they are the right ones to have made. They are the reason the project can still be re-architected rather than restarted.

The problems are not in those commitments. They are in three places:

**The model is driven through a 2023-era text protocol.** Every provider adapter accepts a `tools=` argument and ignores it. Tool calls are regex-parsed `MARKER: argument` lines, one string argument per call, one action per step. The entire conversation is flattened into a single user message with `[role]` prefixes; the model never sees an assistant/tool alternation, never sees a tool's description or schema, and never gets a stable prompt prefix because the clock-to-the-minute is the first line of the system prompt. The 1,942-line session runner then polices the model's prose with seven families of regex for hallucinated results, invented tools, mid-sentence markers, and claims of commits or TV actions that never happened. Every one of those heuristics is a live-caught incident that native structured tool calling would have made impossible. This is the single largest source of accidental complexity and the single largest cap on reasoning quality, and it is also the most tractable fix.

**The self-improvement loop is open.** The event that is supposed to close it, `learn.self_patch.applied`, is published only by a pipeline whose trigger topic nothing publishes; the path that actually lands Sim's code publishes nothing about it. Four subsystems subscribe to an event that never fires. Competence learning records 91% of outcomes as `unknown` because chat turns have no task type. The Self Model is mutated in memory only and forgets everything at restart. Reflection's findings reach the model as one line of prose. There is no path today by which an outcome changes future behaviour. "Self-improving" is, at present, a property of the creator's process, not of the system.

**The substrate is sized for a cluster and billed to a laptop.** Per-message trace streams have produced 118,215 files (88,356 of them traces, 76% holding one event); every append is fsync'd; "forever" streams have no retention path because it needs a snapshot nobody takes; 85% of every Guardian decision ever made is dashboard WebRTC keepalive traffic for the Ring camera; one tool call costs about thirteen bus messages and twenty fsync'd file writes; three bus backends, four ledger backends, a multi-process worker kernel and a distributed lease protocol are carried by a system that runs one process with one worker. None of this is wrong in the abstract. All of it is paid for on every turn.

Beneath those three there is a fourth pattern that explains the project's own most-reported bug shape, the "unconnected wire": the boundaries were drawn early and correctly, but the enforcement stops at the import graph. Topics, config keys, reversibility labels, manifests and schemas can all be declared on one side and never consumed on the other, and nothing fails. Twenty-five topics have one side. Guardian trusts the reversibility label the proposer chose. Interface's manifest lists half of what it subscribes to. The fix is not more discipline; it is making the contract checks fail the build.

The safety picture deserves a plain statement. The bus-level topology is excellent and verified. But the live default auto-approves every irreversible action (set by the Kernel, not by `sim.sh`); `run_shell` is on by default and the protected-path list does not cover `~/.simorgh/secrets.toml`, the ledger, `.git/hooks` or `tests/`; skills are arbitrary persistent code labelled "reversible"; four call sites in Execution run tools with no proposal at all; the camera stills and live HLS are served without the token on a `0.0.0.0` bind; and a door lock is gated by exactly the same boolean as a docstring edit. None of these is a hole in the design. Each is a place where the design was not carried to the edge.

**The recommendation, in one paragraph.** Keep the substrate commitments (one shared dependency, structural approval, event log, worktree landing, loader). Replace the marker protocol with native tool calling and a real message transcript, and delete the regex police with it. Give conversation a session. Close the learning loop by having the landing path publish the outcome and by making competence gate behaviour. Move state that is not an audit trail out of per-file JSONL into SQLite, trace per turn rather than per message, and take the Ring signalling off the approval path. Carry the safety design to the edges with a physical-action tier that always asks a human. Then replace shape-testing with a small set of end-to-end assertions and a daily-path regression benchmark. The migration in section 11 does this in stages, each of which leaves the system running.

## 2. What Simorgh actually is today

Everything here was measured on 2026-09-18 from the working tree and the live data directory; the commands are in section 14.

| Dimension | Measured |
|---|---|
| Code | 86,996 lines, 383 files, 18 subsystem packages + `contracts` |
| Tests | 90,203 lines, 447 files; 44 integration files, 33 of which boot a `Kernel` |
| Docs | 26,150 lines of Markdown (EVOLUTION 5,254; blueprint 9,095; plans 5,923) |
| Prose inside source | 28.5% of non-blank lines are docstrings or comments; 1,118 comments are dated incident notes |
| Retired v1 | `src/` 16,441 lines + 41 test files (887 tests), imported by nothing |
| Topics / schemas | 174 message types (37 replies); 111 have both sides, 25 have one side or none |
| Tools | 104 classes, 98 registered; CHAT profile binds 72, VOICE_CHAT 58, PATCH 25 |
| Providers | Together (primary), Claude Code CLI, Gemini, Ollama (chat-only fallback), plus a deterministic floor |
| Backends built | bus: memory, sqlite, aws; ledger: jsonl, sqlite, dynamodb, memory |
| Backends in force | bus `memory`, ledger `jsonl`, mode `single`, one worker |
| Ledger on disk | 1.4 GB: 118,215 stream files + 90,755 idempotency files; 88,356 trace streams, 26,737 action streams, 2,431 task streams |
| Largest streams | `metrics:history` 114 MB (a full snapshot every 10 s), `curiosity:ticks` 43 MB (an "autonomy paused" event every 3 s), `persona:state` 17 MB (mood decay every 5 s) |
| Actions ever proposed | 26,737; 22,849 (85%) are `ring_live` offer/keepalive/close from the dashboard; next: `cam_stream` 721, `run_shell` 570, `read_file` 473, `search_code` 431 |
| Guardian decisions | sample of 3,000: 2,995 approved, 5 denied; escalations to a human: 0 in 26,737 |
| Learning signal | 2,714 outcome rows: `unknown` 2,466 (91%), research 125, patch 81, skill 3 |
| Sim's own commits | 94 of 856, +8,069 / -512 lines, landed through worktrees |
| Workspace | 11 GB in the checkout (voice 6.4 GB, cameras 3.8 GB) |
| Voice latency (live, 2026-09-18) | STT 1.8 to 6.8 s, LLM 1.3 to 9.5 s, full response 4 to 17 s |
| Boot gate | ~45 s core suite; skipped by hand on 34 of the last 70 boots |

### 2.1 The shape of the system

```
People ── Interface (CLI/TUI/HTTP/Telegram/WhatsApp) ── Voice ──┐
                                                                 │ percept.text.received
                                                                 ▼
                     Orchestration (1 worker) ── Session runner ── cognition.think ──▶ Cognition ──▶ provider
                                    │                                                  (markers in free text)
                                    │ action.proposed
                                    ▼
                                 Guardian (12 rules, HMAC) ── action.approved ──▶ Execution (98 tools, re-verifies)
                                                                                       │ action.result
                     Learning / Reflection / Curiosity / World Model / Persona ◀───────┘   (observers)
                     Ledger: one JSONL file per stream, fsync per append; Bus: in-memory, 175 topics
```

Three facts about this picture are load-bearing for everything that follows:

- **The import rule holds.** A grep of `from simorgh.X` across all fifteen non-substrate packages finds only `bus`, `ledger` and `contracts`; `tests/simorgh/test_module_boundaries.py` enforces it. This is rare and valuable.
- **The action path is structural.** `contracts/topics.py` reserves `action.proposed` to Guardian and `action.approved` to Execution as bus-enforced policy; Execution refuses to start without the HMAC secret and re-derives the token from the ledger's own `received` event before running anything. Every one of the 26,737 recorded actions went through it.
- **Everything else is a broadcast.** Of 157 subscriptions, five use the at-least-once lane (ack, retry, dead-letter, backpressure). The other 152 are drop-on-error broadcasts with unbounded queues, up to 16 handlers concurrently, and no ordering unless the publisher set a partition key, which only 32 sites do.

## 3. What went right

These are the decisions to keep. Each was verified in the code, and each is the kind of decision that is very hard to retrofit.

1. **One shared dependency, enforced.** `simorgh/contracts` is the only thing subsystems share, and a test fails if that changes. Every merge or split proposed in Part II is possible because of this.

2. **Proposal, approval and effect are three different publishers, and the bus refuses anything else.** Guardian is the only subscriber to `action.proposed`; Execution is the only subscriber to `action.approved`; Execution can publish `action.denied` only with `layer: "token"`. A model, a bug or a compromised handler cannot route around it from inside the bus. The HMAC token is ceremony within one process, but it has caught real replay and redelivery bugs, and it is exactly what makes a future multi-process split safe.

3. **Self-modification happens in a worktree and lands through a gate.** Patch and skill tasks branch, commit there, rebase, run the suite, and fast-forward main. Ninety-four Sim-authored commits have landed this way. The live checkout is never edited by a task of those kinds.

4. **The bootloader is the undo mechanism, and it is protected from the thing it undoes.** `simloader.py` gates each boot, tags known-good commits, steps back on failure, and the gate has learned from three demonstrated attacks: exit code must be zero, the summary must not report failures, tests must actually have run, and the test count may not shrink more than 10% from the last green baseline. `sim.sh` restores the loader from the last good tag if it will not compile. Corrigibility is implemented, not declared.

5. **Honest floors and honest health.** A provider being unreachable degrades to a deterministic answer, never a hang. Learning reports `degraded` with the exact reason; Ledger reports `down` when it cannot persist. Silent handler failure was institutionalised as a stderr print with the dated incidents that justify it. A prompt whose memory block failed says so to the model rather than pretending the store was empty.

6. **Boot is layered and health-gated.** No worker can claim a task before Guardian and Execution are up. Shutdown is reverse order.

7. **The tool layer's safety primitives are good where they exist.** `pathsafety` closes symlink, hardlink and case-folding bypasses; `run_container` does not bind-mount the repo and allow-lists image prefixes; `run_remote` takes host and key from the operator's environment, never from the model; Telegram is deny-by-default; the HTTP API has a bearer token.

8. **The two-recall memory block and the supersession header** are a genuinely thoughtful answer to "which memory wins when two disagree," even if the retrieval beneath them is weak.

9. **The project measures itself.** `docs/findings/`, the trial harness, observer waves, the benchmark unit with per-model history, and a retrospective that concluded its own unit tests were not catching real failures. Very few projects reach that conclusion about themselves.

10. **The stated principles are the right ones.** "Sim does not speak to devices, Sim speaks to Home Assistant," "the undo mechanism is not the system's to edit," "a tool must never succeed while saying nothing true." Part of this review is simply pointing at places where the code has not yet caught up with the principles.

---

## 4. Where it went wrong: the structural mistakes

Nine sections, seven mistakes: 4.1 to 4.3 are three faces of one decision about how the model is driven. Ordered by how much they cost per day and how much they cap future capability. Each has been verified against the code by at least two independent readers and by hand; file references are to `main` at `38a9049`.

### 4.1 The model is driven through a text-marker protocol, not native tool calling

**What is there.** `cognition/providers/{together,claude_code,ollama,gemini}.py` each declare `complete(messages, *, tools, ...)` and none of them sends `tools` to the API; `cognition/service.py` passes `tools=None` on every call. The model is told the upper-cased names of its tools plus hand-written argument hints and asked to write `TOOL_NAME: argument` as the first line of its reply. `cognition/parser.py::_parse_markers` extracts at most one string argument per marker; `orchestration/tools.py` keeps five hand-maintained tables to remap that one string onto each tool's real schema, with a second-line JSON hack for multi-argument tools. The model never sees a tool's `description` or `args_schema`, both of which exist on every tool class.

**What it costs.**
- `orchestration/session.py` carries `invented_markers`, `unhonoured_marker`, `_transcript_echo`, `claimed_to_commit`, `promised_behaviour`, `claimed_tv_act` and `claimed_to_note_a_pronunciation`: seven regex families, each added after a live incident in which the model fabricated a result, described a tool call in prose, put a marker mid-sentence, or claimed an effect that no tool produced. Native tool calling makes every one of those failure modes structurally impossible: a tool call is a typed object or it is not a tool call.
- One action per step. Read-only batches are the exception (`_read_batch`) and default off. A modern loop issues several tool calls per turn.
- The model invents argument shapes because it has never been shown one. The project's own comment at `tools.py:241-265` describes the "bare `KeyError`" class of failure this causes.
- Provider-native tags (`<tool_call>`) leak into replies and have to be stripped (`parser.py:148`).

**Why it happened.** The marker vocabulary was inherited from v1 ("v1's full 14-marker conversational set", `tools.py:6`) when Together's function calling was less reliable, and it kept the floor provider and Ollama on one code path. That was a reasonable 2025 choice. It is not a 2026 one: every provider in the router supports structured tool use, and the Claude Code CLI provider is literally a tool-using agent being asked to write markers.

**Fix.** Section 8.1. Send `tools` as JSON schema (the schemas already exist), receive typed `tool_use` blocks, return results as `tool_result` messages, allow N calls per turn, delete the seven regex families and the five remap tables. Keep the marker parser only as a fallback for the floor provider and for models with no tool support, and make that fallback explicit in the provider's capability flags.

### 4.2 The transcript is flattened into one user message

**What is there.** The session runner keeps a real assistant/user alternation in `session.messages` (`session.py:1027-1046`), and that is where the good design stops. `cognition/compaction.py:153` renders every segment as `"\n\n".join(f"[{role}] {content}")` (the assembler does the same at `assembler.py:70` for budgeting), and `cognition/service.py:340` sends that string as a single `user` message after two `system` messages. Tool results are appended as a user turn reading "Result of read_file: ...". The provider never sees an assistant/user/tool alternation; it is asked to continue a conversation rendered as a transcript inside one turn.

**What it costs.** Models are trained on the alternation; the project's own comment (`session.py`, "Two turns, not one") records a live failure where the model lost the thread because a tool result was attributed to itself. Flattening also defeats prompt caching entirely and makes compaction harder than it needs to be, because the thing being compacted is a string rather than a list of typed messages.

**Fix.** Keep `session.messages` as real messages all the way to the provider. This is a small change once 4.1 is done, and it is a prerequisite for prompt caching, for sub-agent context isolation, and for replaying a session from the ledger.

### 4.3 No stable prompt prefix, so no prompt caching

**What is there.** `orchestration/scaffolds.py:638,690-692` renders "Right now it is Friday 18 September 2026, 21:14." and prepends it to the protected `task_rules` block. Four small protected blocks sit before it (constitution, persona voice, self summary, user profile: a few hundred tokens together), so a short stable prefix exists; everything from the clock onward, which is the bulk of the system message, changes every minute. The remaining-steps hint changes every step. The persona line changes with every five-second mood decay.

**What it costs.** Every provider that supports prefix caching (Together for supported models, Anthropic, Gemini) gets a cache miss on most of the prompt every minute. With the CHAT profile now binding 72 tools and the assembler sending memory, persona, self-summary, user-profile and task-rules blocks on every turn, the cacheable prefix could be most of the prompt.

**Fix.** Order blocks stable-first (identity, tool schemas, task rules), put the clock and the budget hint at the end of the user turn, and measure cache hit rate as a Cognition metric.

### 4.4 The self-improvement loop is open

This is the finding that matters most for the project's stated purpose, and it was found independently by two readers and verified by hand.

**What is there.**
- `learn.self_patch.applied` is published in exactly one place, `learning/pipeline.py:196`, inside `PatchPipeline`, which runs only on `learn.pipeline.run`. Nothing in `simorgh/` publishes `learn.pipeline.run`. World Model, Curiosity, Reflection and Planning all subscribe to `learn.self_patch.applied`. The path that actually lands Sim's code, `orchestration/session.py::_land`, publishes nothing about the landing.
- The same pipeline dispatches `tool="self_patch.draft"` (`pipeline.py:74`), which is not in the registry. Already known; restated because it is the same dead pipeline.
- `learning/outcomes.py` derives task type from the first event of `task:<id>`; chat turns have a `task.completed` but no created event, so 2,466 of 2,714 rows are `unknown` with `succeeded=True`. The Self Model's competence section reads "unknown 97%".
- The Self Model is mutated in memory (`worldmodel/selfmodel.py`) and never folded from a stream; a restart forgets competence, limitations and change history. `SELF.md` v42 shows change history "(none recorded yet)" after 94 landed commits.
- The only consumer of a competence estimate is one rendered line in the self-summary prompt block. No routing, no step budget, no profile choice, no tier escalation reads it.
- Curiosity's throttle reads `budget.remaining_fraction` and `budget.free` from a provider-status payload that carries `calls/max_calls/spend_usd/...`, so it never throttles.

**What it costs.** The architecture has a growth layer of three packages (4,539 lines) and a Self Model whose purpose is to make the next task go better than the last. Today the measurable effect of that layer on behaviour is zero, while it costs bus traffic, ledger growth (45 MB of paused-curiosity ticks) and prompt tokens.

**Fix.** Section 8.5: the landing path publishes the outcome; outcomes carry a task type and a verdict or are not recorded; the Self Model is a projection folded from `learn:outcomes` and `self:changes` at boot; competence gates something concrete (tier, budget, whether to ask before acting); Reflection's findings become prompt or policy deltas with an owner and an expiry.

### 4.5 Conversation has no session; memory is asked to be the transcript

**What is there.** `interface/service.py` mints a fresh `session_id` per typed line (correctly, as a reply-correlation key). Voice mints one per spoken turn. Telegram and WhatsApp keep one per chat in memory only. The orchestration `Session` is a task-attempt record. The designed `WorkingMemory` kind has no producer. So "what we were just saying" is reconstructed every turn by `orchestration/context.py::_memory_block`: a similarity recall of eight items and a recency recall of six, from a store whose embeddings are a 256-bucket sha256 bag of words (`memory/embed.py`) that scores `"stop the loop"` against `"halting a runaway iteration"` at 0.000, scoring every record on every call (`memory/store.py:238`, by design), under a 0.25 s budget that is exceeded once the store is large or the machine is busy, at which point the block silently disappears and the model is told its memory "could not be consulted".

**What it costs.** The measured 22-turn session in the project's own notes: a fact told at turn 2 was not available at turns 14 and 19; a correction at turn 9 was overridden by the superseded value four times. This is the family's daily experience of Sim, and it is the reason "Sim forgets" is the complaint the earlier reviews all converged on.

**Fix.** Section 8.4: a conversation object per channel and person, with a rolling transcript window that is in the prompt by construction, compaction into a session summary, and memory as the second tier behind it. Precomputed embeddings in a SQLite index (a real local model, loaded once at boot, off the hot path), so recall is a lookup rather than a scan and the 0.25 s budget stops deciding which embedder the system is allowed to use.

### 4.6 The substrate is sized for a cluster and paid for on every turn

**What is there.**
- Trace storage keyed by `trace_id` plus a fresh uuid per uncaused publish: 88,356 trace streams, 76% with one event, 46k new files a day, none older than two days (retention works only for traces). A chat turn's own trace is a two-event island; there is no end-to-end trace for the daily path.
- `jsonl` ledger, fsync per append, one file plus one idempotency file per stream: 208,970 files, 575 MB of data occupying 1.44 GB.
- `DEFAULT_RETENTION` names only trace/dead/activity; every other stream is "forever", and the forever path is a no-op without a snapshot, of which one exists. `metrics:history` grows ~19 MB per day of uptime.
- One tool call: `action.proposed` → Guardian (2 appends) → `action.approved` → Execution (read-back + 3 appends) → `action.result` + `tool.invoked` + inflight + step records: ~13 bus messages, ~20 fsync'd writes.
- `ring_live`: 22,849 full proposals in five days, one HMAC token and three ledger events each, for WebRTC keepalives.
- Compaction's blob sweep reads every stream file synchronously on the event loop 30 s after boot and every 6 h; the in-memory bus wakes ~170 lanes every 5 ms (~34k idle coroutine resumptions per second).
- Consumer groups, claim RPC, lease heartbeats and a per-second lease scan, for `workers=1` on the in-memory bus. Three bus backends, four ledger backends, `WorkerKernel`, identity tokens, a schema translator registry with zero translators, and a JSON-schema projection of 174 types "for a non-Python subsystem one day".

**Why it happened.** The blueprint designed for `single` / `local-multi` / `aws` from day one so that "the topology can collapse" later. The topology never expanded, but the costs of being ready for it are paid at runtime, not just in code volume.

**Fix.** Section 8.6. SQLite as the ledger backend for everything that is state; JSONL only for the audit streams that must be greppable; retention on every stream by default; traces as spans per turn in one rotating file; Ring signalling off the approval path; freeze or delete the unused backends and the multi-process kernel until the day they are needed, keeping the interfaces.

### 4.7 Safety is structural at the bus and porous at the edges

**What is there.** Each item verified by hand.
- `kernel/service.py:203` sets `irreversible_requires_human = False` unless the config says otherwise; the live config has no `[guardian]` section. Result: zero escalations in 26,737 decisions. The earlier fact-check was right that `sim.sh` does not set this; it missed that the Kernel does.
- `execution/config.py:193`: `shell: bool = True` since 2026-09-07. `run_shell` has been called 570 times. The module map's "off unless configured" is stale.
- `DEFAULT_PROTECTED_SUBJECTS` is twelve repo-relative substrings. `~/.simorgh/secrets.toml` (every provider token), `~/.simorgh/ledger` (the audit trail), `.git/hooks`, `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws` and `tests/` are not in it. `ProtectedRule` is a substring scan of path-looking tokens in the proposal text; its own docstring says a path assembled from pieces defeats it, and `worktree_land` does not re-check the diff that lands.
- `tests/` is inside `write_scopes_source`; the landing gate treats pytest exit 5 (nothing collected) as success and does not check the summary or a run-count baseline, while the loader's gate does all three. So a patch task can weaken the tests it is gated by, land, and be caught only at the next boot, if the gate is not skipped.
- `apply_skill` and every `skill:<name>` tool are labelled `reversible`, so persistent arbitrary code is auto-allowed even with the human gate on.
- Guardian builds `ToolInfo` from the proposal's own `reversibility` field and never consumes `tool.registered`; the proposer chooses its own label.
- `execution/service.py:484,517,543,561` call `tool.run()` directly with synthetic action ids (TV cast at boot, charts, camera streams); the camera watcher does the same. These effects have no proposal, no token and no `action:` stream.
- `sim_command` lets the model run any typed CLI line through `ui.command.request` (a topic with no publish policy) into `dispatch()`; Guardian sees only the wrapper. `skills` mutates disk outside the action path.
- `interface/dashfeeds.py` (1,110 lines, on by default) performs outbound HTTP with a spoofed user agent from the surfaces layer, outside Execution and Guardian.
- `interface/httpapi.py:922`: `/tv/hls/`, `/tv/media/`, `/wallpapers/` and `/cameras/snap/` are exempt from the token; the live bind is `0.0.0.0`. Anyone on the LAN can watch the house.
- The 21 house/camera/Ring tools and 17 TV/media tools use the same `reversibility` constant and the same rule as a file edit. There is no physical-action tier.
- `simorgh/interface/dispatch.py` writes MCP approvals to a cwd-relative `simorgh.toml`, which the Kernel's search order prefers over `~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml`; a stray write shadows the real config at next boot.

**Fix.** Section 8.6 and 9: a physical-action tier that always asks; protected subjects as resolved absolute paths including the data directory, the vault, the ledger, the hooks and the test tree; the landing gate reusing the loader's verdict function; Guardian owning the reversibility class from the registry; every effect through the path, including boot-time casts and dashboard signalling (once, per session); token on every route that shows the inside of the house.

### 4.8 Verification certifies shape, not behaviour

**What is there.**
- The suite is larger than the code and mostly in-process with faked collaborators; the project's own retrospective says it missed every real blocker. 41 top-level test files (887 tests, 11.5k lines) test the retired `src/` tree and are still in `--all-tests` and in the "all" baseline.
- The loader's docstring says a known-good tag is earned by "the unit suite plus the scored trial suite"; `run_gate` runs trials only under `--full`, and the decision log shows unit-only blesses. The gate was skipped by hand on 34 of the last 70 boots.
- Five of Verification's eleven mechanical checks (denylist_immunity, docstring, invariants, isolated_suite, sandbox_smoke) can never run on the real path because the verify subject never carries `candidate/code/original` and the wire kind is always `task`. `full_suite_ran` demands all ~6,000 tests inside every patch task and has failed 56 of 62 times.
- `Supervisor.poll_once` (the only path to restart and to auto-pause on Guardian down) has no production caller; `health_every_s` is parsed and never read; `_restart` stops a service and never starts it.
- Logging is never configured; every subsystem's INFO log is dropped.
- No regression benchmark exists for the daily path (chat and voice latency, prompt size, memory-block presence, trace-writer drops).

**Fix.** Section 8.7 and 10: three end-to-end assertions that drive real subsystems with only the provider faked; a daily-path benchmark that runs nightly against a ledger copy; delete the v1 tests with v1; make the gate's verdict function the one gate; a Supervisor that actually ticks.

### 4.9 Boundaries drifted where the import rule could not see

- `execution` is 21.6k lines holding six product domains next to the HMAC verifier; the most trusted subsystem is the largest and the one with the most churn.
- `session.py` hard-codes the TV tool list, TV and dashboard claim regexes, a pronunciation regex, misheard forms of Sim's name and a voice-only refusal rule; `Session` carries speaker, room and channel.
- `contracts` now contains five modules that run git, write log files under a lock and read/write `simorgh.toml`, plus four of the codebase's nine module-level mutable singletons.
- Typed config is read via `getattr(config, "x", default)` at 123 sites; in 20 of them the fallback contradicts the dataclass default.
- 25 topics have one side or none; Interface's `consumes`/`produces` manifest lists 16 and 12 while the package subscribes 33 times.
- `Persona` writes a ledger event and a bus message every 5 s of mood decay (93% of its 47,784 events) and adds a 2 s-timeout bus round trip to every prompt to inject one sentence.
- Voice is two half-generations: `VoiceSession` reaches into the legacy `Pipeline` 29 times; the echo canceller is wired into a loop the live path never runs; barge-in is off in production.
- The retired v1 (16k lines), 11 GB of `workspace/`, 109 MB of `papers/`, `games/`, `images/` and `results/` live in the checkout; `simorgh/big.py` is a two-line stray.

None of these is dangerous alone. Together they are why a change in one place needs a dated comment explaining what it will break somewhere else.

---

## 5. On the previous reviews

Three prior documents exist: an external second-opinion review, a fact-check of it, and an audit written from both. This evaluation agrees with the fact-check on every point it checked, and adds these corrections to the picture they left:

- The CHAT profile binds **72** tools today, not 34. The count moved during the same day the fact-check was written. The revised audit (its section 3.2) has this right.
- Auto-approve of irreversible actions **is** the live default. `sim.sh` does not set it; `kernel/service.py:203` does, with `guardian_section.setdefault("irreversible_requires_human", False)`, and the live config has no `[guardian]` section to override it. The revised audit's section 3.6 ("actual runtime default: human approval required; the system is safer than its docs claim") is wrong on this point: `docs/architecture.md` was describing the Kernel's behaviour correctly, only attributing it to the wrong file. The evidence is the ledger itself: zero escalations in 26,737 decisions.
- `run_shell` is **on** by default, not "off unless configured".
- The self-improvement loop is not merely missing a tool (`self_patch.draft`); its closing event is never published by the path that lands code.
- "Conversational amnesia" has a deeper cause than the missing buffer: the embedder is chosen by a 0.25 s timeout, the recall is a full scan, and the block vanishes silently under load.
- The audit's proposal to merge Cognition and Orchestration into one `reasoning/` layer is close to right but for the wrong reason (bus latency is not the cost); section 9 gives the version of it that fixes the actual problem.
- The audit's proposal to "migrate to SQLite WAL" is right, but the larger win is stopping per-message trace files and adding retention, which no backend swap fixes on its own.

---

## 6. Answering the question directly: where did I go wrong?

Not in the places that are hardest to fix. The boundaries, the gate, the log, the loader and the principles are right. The mistakes were:

1. **Building the substrate for the third deployment before the first one worked**, and paying its runtime costs on a laptop.
2. **Keeping v1's text-marker protocol into v2** instead of adopting native tool calling when the providers made it reliable, and then spending weeks of incident-driven heuristics compensating for it.
3. **Treating the growth layer as three packages to build rather than one loop to close.** Learning, Reflection and Curiosity were each built to their spec; the wire from "a patch landed" to "the Self Model changed" to "behaviour changed" was never asserted end to end, and it is not connected.
4. **Letting the conversation be a memory query.** A session is a first-class object in every agent system that people talk to daily; here it was left to recall.
5. **Enforcing boundaries at the import graph only.** Topics, labels, manifests and config keys are contracts too, and nothing fails when one side is missing. That is the "unconnected wire" bug shape, and it is a tooling gap, not a discipline gap.
6. **Letting incidents drive design.** The 1,118 dated comments and the seven regex families are the trace of a process that fixed each live failure where it appeared rather than at its cause. That process produced a working system fast; it is now the thing making the system hard to change.
7. **Writing the safety design to the bus and not to the edges.** The gate is excellent; the defaults, the protected list, the direct calls and the open routes are where it leaks.

Everything in Part II follows from fixing these seven in the order that lets each fix make the next one smaller.


---

# Part II: Where agents are going, and how to re-architect Sim to get there

Part II answers the second question. It was produced by a design panel: four independent architects each wrote a complete re-architecture from a different lens (the modern agent harness; cognitive architecture and long-horizon autonomy; production systems and evaluation; the embodied household agent), three independent judges scored all four and resolved their contradictions, and a synthesiser produced one target architecture from the winning spine with the best-scored ideas grafted in. Every claim about Sim's current code in this part was re-verified against the tree during that process. The judges' scores and the disagreements they resolved are summarised in 14.3.

The harness lens won on all three scorecards (total 40 to 43 of 50), conditional on three things the judges insisted on: physical-safety closure and the zero-contract wires go first; native tool calling and streaming land in the first quarter rather than at the end; and the physical package consolidation is deferred to the last stage and gated by the eval suite. That is the plan below.

---

## 7. Where the field is, and where Sim stands

By 2026 the shape of a capable agent is no longer contested. The patterns below are the ones every serious harness has converged on. For each, the table says what Sim has, honestly.

| Pattern | What it means | Sim today |
|---|---|---|
| **Native structured tool use** | Tools are JSON-schema declarations sent to the model; the model returns typed `tool_use` blocks; results return as `tool_result` blocks keyed by id; several calls per turn | Not used. Markers in prose, one string argument, one call per step. Every tool already has the schema. |
| **A typed, persisted transcript** | The unit of state is a list of turns of typed blocks; it is what gets compacted, resumed, replayed and evaluated | Task attempts have step records on the ledger; chat and voice have nothing; the provider sees one flattened string |
| **Context management under token pressure** | Old tool results aged into re-fetchable stubs; a structured progress note when the window fills; a stable cacheable prefix | A five-layer compactor exists and a good progress-note shape exists, triggered by step count (measured as no gain); no cacheable prefix |
| **Agent definitions as permission modes** | An agent is tools + model tier + budget + system prompt + isolation, declared as data; hooks at fixed points (pre-tool, post-tool, stop, pre-compact) | Profiles and scaffolds are exactly this, reached from the other side; Guardian is the pre-tool hook nobody can remove. Not yet files, not yet protected. |
| **Sub-agents with isolated context** | Delegation to a child with a fresh context, its own budget, summary-only return | Built (`delegate`), off by default; projects never produce a child that completes |
| **Skills as procedural memory** | Reusable procedures as files the model reads on demand, diffable, protectable | Built in the open SKILL.md format with catalog-then-load. Nothing promotes the ones Reflection drafts. |
| **Tiered memory with real retrieval** | Working (transcript), episodic (indexed at write), semantic (facts with supersession and provenance), procedural (skills); hybrid lexical + dense retrieval; recall also as a tool | Episodic and semantic stores exist; hashing embeddings; full scan per recall; supersession by a prose header |
| **Model routing by purpose and tier** | Cheap models for classification and summaries, strong models for planning and review, escalation on failure, per-purpose reasoning effort | The router, budgets, failover and tier mechanism exist and are well built; the routes map is unset; everything runs on the cheapest model at low effort |
| **Streaming end to end** | Deltas to the surface and to TTS; first audio after the first sentence | Streaming synthesiser and player are built and receive nothing; no provider streams |
| **MCP as the integration standard** | New external capability arrives as a server with schemas, not a subsystem | A client exists; tools with more than one property are uncallable through the marker layer |
| **Eval-driven development** | Capability suites with repeats and confidence intervals are the merge gate | Benchmark unit, trial harness and observer kit exist as tools; the gate is a unit suite that asserts shape |
| **Structural permission chokepoint** | Every effect passes one gate the loop cannot skip | Sim's is stronger than the field's norm: bus topology, not a callback |
| **Checkpoint and resume** | Long tasks survive restarts and interruptions without redoing work | Built and proven for tasks; the transcript is not on the ledger, so a resumed session is blind |
| **A world model of the environment** | Entity state, presence, situation, staleness, rendered as data | Facets are codebase-shaped; the house is a 16-line deque in the voice session |
| **One identity across surfaces** | A person is one person in the kitchen, on Telegram and at the terminal, with a memory namespace and permissions | Four ad-hoc session models; identity only on the voice path |

Read down the third column and the pattern is consistent: **Sim has most of the machinery and almost none of it is connected or switched on.** That is a much better position than the reverse. The plan below is mostly wiring, ordering and deletion, with three genuine builds (native tools, the session stream, the memory tiers) and one genuine merge (the growth loop).

---

## 8. The target architecture

### 8.0 In one paragraph

Keep the substrate (Bus, Ledger, Kernel, Contracts) and the safety path (Guardian, Execution with its token verifier, Verification, worktree landing, the loader) as they are, and close the verified safety gaps in week one. The thinking path becomes one loop for every session kind (chat, voice, task, project, sub-agent) over a typed transcript persisted as a `session:<id>` ledger stream; native JSON-schema tools rendered per provider dialect behind capability flags with the marker protocol frozen as the fallback; N tool calls per turn (reads concurrent, writes serialised), each proposed to Guardian as the mandatory pre-tool hook; one context builder with a cacheable prefix; compaction by measured token pressure; streaming deltas to the terminal and to Voice's already-built sentence synthesiser; agent definitions as Guardian-protected files with hooks; a `Task` built-in for in-process sub-agents; budgets in tokens, dollars and wall-clock. Cognition becomes an LLM gateway. Memory becomes four real tiers. World Model becomes two durable projections (a Self Model of estimated quantities; a `world:home` of entity state and presence) plus a People store. Guardian gains tiers 0 to 3 with tier 3 always human. Telemetry leaves the decision log. Learning, Reflection and Curiosity merge into one growth loop whose only output is a proposal through the gate, adopted only when a held-out eval improves. Benchmark, the trial harness and the observer kit merge into an evals package that is the loader's bless gate. Nothing acts on the world except through `action.proposed`; nothing loosens a gate except a human.

"From" says what happens to today's packages. Topics are preserved wherever a package merges, so no consumer changes.

### 8.2 Merges

- `learning` + `reflection` + `curiosity` → `growth/` (one loop over a policy store; topics preserved).
- `benchmark` + `tools/trial.py` + `tools/trial_suite.py` + `tools/observer_kit.py` + `tools/bench_instance.py` → `evals/` (the gate).
- `bus/trace.py` + `kernel/metrics.py` + the read side of `interface/dashfeeds.py` → `telemetry/`.
- `cognition/assembler.py` block order + `orchestration/context.py` → one ContextBuilder in orchestration (the decision the project already took in its own post-cutover review, section 3.2).
- `profiles.py` + `scaffolds.py` → `agents/<name>.md` definitions.
- `curiosity/sharing.py` + `persona/sharing.py` + the announce step in `execution/vision.py` + reminder delivery + backchannel greetings → `initiative/`.

- The voice session's room deque + `contracts/places.py` → the `world:home` facet.

- Guardian `HomeRule` recomputing `classify_call`; `[guardian.physical]` posture; requester on proposals; the physical self-check drill (week one).
- `ToolSpec` on `tool.registered` with the schema serialised; per-provider dialect rendering; JSON-schema validation; tool-use and tool-result turns; parallel blocks; provider capability flags; a direct Anthropic Messages API adapter.
- `session:<id>` ledger stream with typed turns; persistent sessions per (channel, person); resume from stream.
- Streaming provider interface; `session.delta`; the voice sentence chunker; streaming STT as primary; fast-lane acknowledgements; a deadline in the envelope with per-stage budgets.

- Token-pressure compactor (result aging with `recall_result` stubs, then the progress note); budgets in tokens, USD and wall-clock.
- `agents/<name>.md` definitions with hooks; `Task`, `memory_search`, `recall_result` and `plan` built-ins; planner, skill-writer, verify and browser agent definitions.
- Memory: warmed dense embedder, persisted vectors, BM25 + reciprocal rank fusion, fact store with supersession, per-person digest, speculative recall on percept.
- `self:model` fold with Beta posteriors, calibration, tool reliability, provider quality; `compute_gaps` implemented; `capabilities.tools` written.
- `world:home` projection, presence belief, situation facts, the "world now" block.

- `growth:policies` store with eval-gated adoption as committed protected files; Thompson-sampled exploration; nightly capped eval loop; routine mining once HA history exists.
- `evals/` with repeats, confidence intervals, seq-keyed replay, kill-and-resume and household suites; the loader's bless runs it.
- `telemetry/` spans and samples tables; trace threading per session.
- `pyproject.toml` and `ruff`; HTTP auth on by default for non-loopback binds; logging configured; a Supervisor that ticks.

### 8.4 Deletions and freezes

- The marker protocol: frozen as the fallback dialect for providers without tool support (the Claude Code CLI wrapper, the floor, tool-less local models); no new markers, no new code-bearing entries, no new marker hints.
- The seven regex police: frozen (no new members); each deleted on native paths only when its counter reads zero for a bless cycle; `invented_markers`, `unhonoured_marker` and `_transcript_echo` kept on the fallback dialect.
- `learning/pipeline.py` PatchPipeline, `learn.pipeline.run`, the `draft_candidate` and `self_patch.draft` references: deleted (verified unreachable).
- Per-line throwaway chat sessions: deleted once session streams exist.
- The double prompt assembly and the 0.25 s bus RPCs for prompt blocks: replaced by one builder and injected readers in single mode.
- Step-count re-grounding as a trigger: not turned on (the project's own 2026-09-15 finding measured every-6 as no gain with about double the step exhaustion); replaced by token pressure; the step cap kept only as a sanity bound.
- `flag_contradictions`' symmetric penalty: replaced by supersession; `persona/user_model.py` regex extraction frozen once facts exist.
- `metrics:history`, `curiosity:ticks`, `persona:state` as event streams and `trace:<id>` per message: removed in favour of the samples and spans tables.
- The 8,000-char tool-result cut and the 300 s bus handler timeout as an implicit wall budget: replaced by summary + blob ref and by budgets in the envelope.
- `SIMORGH_GUARDIAN_AUTO_APPROVE` no longer covers physical tools (it may keep covering code).
- Curiosity's repo-area-only target space as the default: household and world unknowns first.
- `src/`: deleted from the tree, tagged. `simorgh/big.py`, `.Rhistory`, `.obsidian/`: removed. `workspace/`, `papers/`, `games/`, `images/`, `results/`: out of the checkout, with retention by age and size for what Sim writes.
- Deferred, not deleted: the SQLite default for the decision log (last stage, with its own eval); STT/TTS engines out of process (only if spans show a stall); the interface split and the `agent/` + `llm/` moves (last stage, gated by evals); the unused bus and ledger backends, `WorkerKernel`, the identity registry and the schema translator (frozen behind their interfaces until a second process exists).

---

## 9. Capability programs

One per capability the creator named. Each says what is there, what method replaces it, how it is measured, and what the first increment is. The first increments are deliberately small: several are configuration.

### 9.1 Reasoning

**Current.** One think per step at low reasoning effort on the cheapest Together model for every purpose; tool calls parsed from prose with a correction turn on every police trigger; no planner/actor/critic separation inside a task; tier escalation exists and is unset; Verification only at task end; the LLM answer reviewer measured as not a net gain; BFCL, GAIA and SWE-bench scored but gating nothing. The leading benchmark failure is "step budget exhausted", not wrong reasoning.

**Method.**
1. Route by purpose and tier first, because it is configuration today: a strong tier for plan, decompose, critique and verify-on-failure; a cheap tier for re-ground, consolidate, classify, acknowledge and addressee; `escalate_from_attempt=1` and escalation on a drifting critic verdict; reasoning effort as a routed parameter per purpose.
2. Native structured tool use removes the parse tax and most correction turns; N tool calls per turn so independent lookups cost one turn.
3. Plan-then-act for tasks whose budget exceeds a threshold: a planner agent definition writes a typed Plan with acceptance criteria; the executing agent keeps a plan block in the protected prefix, updated through the `plan` built-in.
4. A critic only where an oracle exists: Verification as the Stop hook with a bounded revise loop; the checkpoint critic against acceptance criteria at every progress note; a fresh-context verify sub-agent for high-rigor tasks; no free-form reviewer on research.
5. Majority vote of three cheap samples only for yes/no verdicts, never for drafts.
6. Situated context as data: the self summary from posteriors, the world-now and dialogue blocks, the per-person digest, so the model reasons over grounded state rather than prose.

**Measure.** BFCL and BFCL-parallel per model; GAIA and a SWE-bench Verified slice with ≥3 repeats and a bootstrap CI; steps, tokens and dollars per resolved case; wasted-step rate from spans; correction turns per 100 turns; critic precision; a 200-case household request set where wrong-entity actuation must be zero.

**First increment (week one, configuration only).** A `[cognition]` routes map (purpose → tier, with a stronger Together model for review, decompose and verify), `escalate_from_attempt=1`, `parallel_read_tools=4` for research and patch. Run the trial suite and one GAIA slice three times before and after; record in `docs/findings/`. Second increment: `ToolSpec` on the wire and native function calling on Together behind a capability flag, with a BFCL baseline on markers first.

### 9.2 Long tasks

**Current.** Budget is steps per attempt; retries carry a mechanical 220-char-per-step note; re-grounding, clean revisions, delegation and parallel reads are built and off (only parallel reads showed a measurable effect: halved step exhaustion on GAIA level 3); tool results cut at 8,000 chars; no wall-clock or dollar budget; projects mark themselves complete when children are created and never wait; no waiting states; resume distinguishes crash from retry (good); the Self Model is rebuilt from nothing at boot.

**Method.** The session transcript as a ledger stream (checkpoint every turn, resume by fold, an explicit checkpoint event after every irreversible action); budgets in tokens, USD and wall-clock with the step cap as a sanity bound; compaction by measured token pressure (results aged into re-fetchable stubs at 70% of the window, progress note at 85%, protected prefix untouched) for every session kind; the model's own progress note as the carried note across attempts; projects as parent sessions that spawn in-process child sub-agents per plan step and await them by event in DAG order; `WAITING(until | event | human)` with scheduler wake-ups so a task can pause for a calendar event or an answer without holding a worker; the checkpoint critic at every note with re-planning after two drifting verdicts; heavy steps (test suite, containers) as subprocesses with kill-on-deadline; standing intents evaluated by a small event-driven engine once `world:home` exists, never by a model polling.

**Measure.** SWE-bench Verified slice resolved rate at ≥50 turns with three repeats; fraction of tasks finished in one attempt; fraction ending in budget exhaustion; resume-after-kill success (kill -9 mid-task in a repo copy; must continue without redoing steps or repeating an irreversible action); context tokens per turn over a 100-turn run (must plateau); projects that produce and complete children (today zero); wall time for a scripted three-day household goal; intent survival across restart.

**First increment (week one).** Delegation on for research; `parallel_read_tools=4`; the model's progress note as the carried note (`resume.py` already reads `task.progress`); build the kill-and-resume trial and a scripted 60-turn task under `tools/trial.py`. Then the session stream and token-pressure compaction (stage 4), measured on the same scripted task.

### 9.3 Environment interaction

**Current.** 98 tools with real JSON schemas the model never sees; the MCP client works but multi-property tools are uncallable; `browse_page` exists; cameras via RTSP → ffmpeg → HLS with `vision.py` describing whole scenes from inside Execution; Cast and Android TV; Home Assistant not configured; `classify_call` exists but Guardian does not recompute it; one auto-approve knob covers sirens and commits; `camera.event` and `tv.state` are published and folded nowhere the model reads; perception is text only.

**Method.** Safety first (week one): `HomeRule`, the physical posture, requester on every proposal, the boot drill; then tiers 0 to 3 with tier 3 always human. Capability second: `ToolSpec` passthrough with schema validation and per-provider dialects; MCP schemas unflattened and MCP as the default way to add external capability, Guardian-gated like everything else; `ToolResult` as summary + blob ref with progressive disclosure; every tool call a span. World state third: `world:home` as a projection of events already on the bus with presence beliefs and situation facts rendered with staleness, so household questions answer from state and observe-tools return diffs; environment events delivered into the relevant session as environment turns so the agent can act on them under the same gate. Breadth last and contingent on the creator's hardware decision: the HA websocket bridge, `home_automation_*` tier-3 tools, Frigate/go2rtc tracked-object events replacing whole-scene description, a browser agent definition over a snapshot-act loop.

**Measure.** Per-tool success rate and p95 latency from spans; MCP tools callable percentage; BFCL-parallel; first-try argument accuracy on multi-field tools; tier-3 effects that reached Execution without a human (zero, drilled at boot); fraction of household questions answered from state with zero tool calls; false-fresh rate; presence accuracy against a family-corrected diary; the household end-to-end suite completion rate; camera announcements judged "described the event, not the scene" above 90%.

**First increment (week one).** `HomeRule` + `[guardian.physical]` + requester + drill (a day of additive code) and `capabilities.tools` written from `tool.registered`. Week three: publish the full `ToolSpec`, render it to the model, pass MCP schemas through unflattened, and measure how many of the 98 + MCP tools are callable with correct arguments on the first try, before and after.

### 9.4 User interaction

**Current.** Throwaway chat sessions; continuity by bag-of-words recall that silently vanishes under load; `WorkingMemory` unfed; no streaming (voice full response 4 to 17 s, STT the largest stage); persona and self summary fetched by RPC every think; correction turns from the police; person-scoped memory only on voice; identity per channel and never joined; unprompted speech from four uncoordinated sources; addressee and identity by regex inside the voice session.

**Method.** One persistent session per (channel, person) with compaction and a transcript the model sees; streaming deltas to the terminal and into Voice's existing sentence synthesiser (first audio after the first sentence, a spoken filler on a slow tool call); streaming STT as the primary lane; a fast-lane acknowledgement from the cheap tier; a deadline in the envelope with per-stage budgets so the 4 to 17 s spread is attributable; speculative recall issued on percept (on the STT partial for voice) so the model never waits on memory; hybrid retrieval with a fact store whose supersession makes corrections win by structure, an entity-linked facts block and a per-person digest as a protected block; `memory_search` for agentic recall; the People model so the same person is one person in the kitchen, on Telegram and at the terminal, with a memory namespace and role-appropriate permissions; addressee as a scored percept field with silence below threshold; Initiative as the single path for unprompted speech, scored against interruption cost, with presence-aware channel choice and a daily cap; proactive shares appended to the same session as assistant turns so they have context.

**Measure.** Time to first token and first audio per turn class from `voice:turns`; the 30-turn household recall scenario built from the ledger's real failures (recall@k for facts, exact-answer rate for corrections, a fact told to one family member not surfacing to another); correction turns per 100 turns; addressee precision and recall and speaker misattribution on labelled sets corrected from the phone; unprompted utterances per day per person and the fraction marked unwanted; user-visible latency p50/p95 per channel and stage-budget breaches per day.

**First increment (week one).** Feed `WorkingMemory` from `turn.completed` keyed by (person or typed, channel) and render the last six turns before the memory block; build the 30-turn recall scenario and run it before and after (zero new contracts). Stage 3: Together streaming → `session.delta` → sentence chunker → streaming synthesiser, and sherpa streaming STT as primary; measure first audio on the same 50 recorded turns before and after.

### 9.5 Self-improvement

**Current.** Self-patch via worktree landing and the loader works when the creator types `improve`; the autonomous PatchPipeline is unreachable; Reflection drafts skills to a directory nobody promotes; Curiosity explores Sim's own code on idle ticks with a constant gap; `compute_gaps` returns an empty list; the Self Model is in-memory and never records tools; benchmarks have history but gate nothing; competence is fed from self-reported outcomes; the unit suite asserts shape.

**Method.** One eval-driven loop in `growth/`: estimate (Beta posteriors with forgetting per task type and strategy, calibration, tool reliability, fed from verify-backed outcomes and eval pass rates as separate weighted sources) → diagnose (deterministic failure clustering) → propose one typed artifact (task-type rule, skill, routing change, code patch) with evidence references → evaluate on a held-out tagged case set in a worktree with repeats against the stored baseline → adopt only on no regression plus a motivating case fixed, landing as a committed file under a Guardian-protected root through `action.proposed(policy_adopt)` → monitor, retire on TTL or posterior drop with bounded rollback. Thompson sampling over posteriors and world unknowns schedules idle work, with the sampler's diversity kept. Nightly, budget-capped, cheap tier. Household learning through the same shape: routine suggestions from HA history, with a person's yes installed as HA automations; speaker and preference refinement only from verified events. Guardian protects `guardian/`, `contracts/`, `kernel/`, `agents/`, hooks, the rules and skills roots and the evals gate, so the loop can never loosen its own gate.

Three design disputes the panel had, and how they were settled: the policy store (cognitive lens) is the container; eval pass rate (systems lens) is the promotion signal, never self-reported outcomes; "only ever a proposal through the gate" (harness lens) is the safety property. One judge objected to any live prompt self-modification on the grounds that an "only adds restrictions" promise cannot be checked; that objection is met by adopting rules only as committed protected files, A/B'd on the trial suite before they are active, never rendered from a mutable store.

**Measure.** Benchmark and eval trend per week per model; policies adopted vs retired and surviving 30 days; eval delta per adoption on its held-out set; regressions attributed to a policy (zero target); self-patch land rate and loader rollback count; Self Model staleness (tools listed vs registered); competence calibration (stated vs measured) per capability; exploration yield (fraction of curiosity tasks that raised a posterior); routine suggestions accepted vs shown and later disabled; learning-driven changes that reached the house without a person's approval (zero).

**First increment (week one).** Implement `compute_gaps` from the competence table; write `capabilities.tools` from `tool.registered`; delete PatchPipeline; have `_land` publish the landing outcome. Two wires and a deletion, no contract change. Stage 4: promote `evals/` to the loader's default bless gate. Stage 8: wire Reflection's distillation output into `simorgh_skills` with an A/B on the trial suite (skill on vs off) and promote only on improvement; the first task-type rule lands as a file in the protected `agents/` root only after passing that type's held-out cases.

File moves are separated from behaviour changes and pushed to the end. The weeks are estimates for one developer working through coding agents; the order is the point, not the calendar.

**The single biggest risk of the whole plan** is half-migration by one developer working through coding agents. The project's own dominant bug shape is the unconnected wire, and this plan is the largest producer of them there is: two tool protocols, two trace formats, two memory indexes, two budgets, two session models, each half-read by something, on a live checkout that boots the family's assistant. The ordering above is the mitigation and it is not negotiable: safety and the gate before any behaviour change; one stage at a time; each stage's old path deleted before the next begins; native tool use flipped per model only after it beats markers on the model actually in use; and the growth loop adopting nothing until its task type has a held-out set with a baseline.

## 11. On "at some point it can be considered AGI"

All four architects, all three judges and the code agree on this, and it should be said plainly because SOUL.md asks for transparency.

Simorgh is a harness around a frontier model. Its general intelligence is the model's. Nothing in this architecture learns at the weight level, and no loop design gives Sim competence the model it calls does not have. A stronger foundation model behind this harness will look far more capable than a weaker one, and that gap is the model's, not Sim's. What the harness decides is how much of the model's intelligence reaches the world, how reliably, for how long, for whom, and how safely. Under a definition of AGI that requires learning beyond its model, this system will not be AGI, and saying otherwise would contradict its own constitution.

What the architecture *can* deliver, and what "more general" concretely means for a household agent, is five numbers in the ledger that should rise over time:

1. **Coverage.** The fraction of the family's real goals (files, web, calendar, mail, devices, TV, cameras, code) completed end to end without the creator stepping in, from a scripted household suite.
2. **Horizon.** Tasks that span hours, restarts and human interruptions with the same safety profile, from the resume and long-task suites.
3. **Continuity.** Knowing several people across months with corrections that stick and privacy that holds, from the recall scenario.
4. **Transfer.** A skill, rule or fact learned in one task helping on a held-out one, from A/B on the trial suite.
5. **Breadth.** New capability arriving as MCP servers, skills and HA automations rather than subsystems, with a person asked only at tier 3.

This is the blueprint's own stance (section 2.1 of the vision document: generality as a queryable number the Self Model reports, including what Sim still cannot do), and it should stay the only use of the word.

What compounds: the eval suite; the ledger of transcripts, which every future eval and distillation reads; the fact store; the world state; the skills and rules library; the tool schemas; the safety tiers; and the model upgrades that a clean native-tool gateway makes free. What does not compound: regex police, dated incident comments, per-tool argument hacks, bespoke command dispatch, more subsystems, and any growth mechanism not scored by an eval.

Two limits to keep in view. The loop cannot verify its own honesty without external checks (Verification, evals, the family's corrections). And corrigibility must stay outside anything the growth loop can touch, which this plan keeps by Guardian-protecting agent definitions, hooks, the policy roots and the eval gate.

The honest target is the one the embodied lens named: the most trustworthy, most capable, continuously improving personal agent in this house, with zero unapproved physical effects, sub-second first audio, presence and addressee accuracy the family stops noticing, and routines it learnt that still run when it is switched off. If the models keep improving, this is the harness that lets Sim absorb that improvement without another rewrite.

---

## 12. What to do first, in order

If only the first month happens, it should be this, and every item is measured before and after:

1. `HomeRule` + `[guardian.physical]` + requester + the boot drill. A day. House actions stop being auto-approved.
2. HTTP auth on by default; protected subjects extended to the data directory, vault, ledger, hooks and tests. An hour.
3. `_land` publishes the landing; outcomes refuse `unknown`; `compute_gaps`; `capabilities.tools`; delete PatchPipeline. Two wires and a deletion.
4. `WorkingMemory` fed and six turns rendered before the memory block. A day. The machine-names and birthday cases start passing.
5. Routes map, `escalate_from_attempt=1`, delegation for research, `parallel_read_tools=4`. Configuration.
6. The gate: trial suite + benchmark + the 30-turn recall scenario + kill-and-resume, ≥3 repeats, recorded. Then `pyproject.toml`, `ruff`, delete `src/` and the stray files.
7. Retention on every stream; Ring signalling off the approval path; the four direct tool runs through the path; a Supervisor that ticks; logging configured.
8. `ToolSpec` on the wire and rendered to the model; BFCL baseline on markers.

Then stage 2 (native tools) and stage 3 (streaming), which are the two changes the family will feel most.

# Part III: Findings catalogue and method

## 13. Findings catalogue

Every finding below was produced by one of nine independent readers, each assigned one architectural concern and instructed to read code rather than history, then attacked by two independent skeptics: one checking factual correctness against the code as it stands, one checking whether the finding is a real problem at this system's scale (one laptop, one family, one developer). No finding was refuted outright. Where a skeptic corrected a claim, the corrected version is what appears here. Where a skeptic judged the severity overstated, the severity shown is the lowered one; the original is in brackets. Findings already established by the earlier reviews (cameras via ffmpeg, `self_patch.draft` unregistered, empty `capabilities["tools"]`, no dialogue buffer, JSONL ledger size, thin tests in persona/learning/worldmodel) were excluded from the readers' brief and appear only where a reader added something material.

Severity means: **critical** = the stated purpose of the system is not met or a person could be harmed; **high** = daily cost or a capability cap; **medium** = real, fix when in the area; **low** = hygiene.

Kinds: *wrong-design* (a decision that is wrong or over-built for this scale), *undermined* (a right design whose implementation defeats it), *bug*, *over-engineering*, *missing*.

### 13.1 Safety: Guardian, Execution, protected paths, self-modification

| # | Sev | Kind | Finding | Evidence | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | **critical** [prop: high] | wrong-design | The live default auto-approves every irreversible action; the door lock, sirens and the shell run with no human in the loop. Guardian never recomputes the physical class and copies the proposer's label. | `kernel/service.py:203` `setdefault("irreversible_requires_human", False)`; no `[guardian]` in `~/.simorgh/simorgh.toml`; 0 escalations in 26,737 decisions | A separate `[guardian.physical]` posture with `auto_approve=false`; `HomeRule` recomputing `classify_call` from typed args; a boot drill that a mislabelled `lock.unlock` is escalated |

### 13.2 The agent loop: Orchestration, prompt assembly, tool protocol

| # | Sev | Kind | Finding | Evidence | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | **critical** [prop: high] | wrong-design | Tool calls are regex-parsed text markers; native function calling is never used. Every provider passes `tools=None`; the model writes `TOOL: argument` as a first line; one call per message outside read-only batches; the model never sees a tool's description or schema. Contracts anticipated native calls (`ProviderResponse.tool_calls`); no provider implements them. | `cognition/service.py:358, 419`; `providers/together.py:117-135`; `providers/ollama.py:126-155`; `cognition/parser.py` | Section 8.1: `ToolSpec` on the wire, per-provider dialects, typed blocks, markers frozen as the fallback |
| L2 | **critical** [corr: high] | wrong-design | The whole transcript is flattened into one user message: the compactor renders every message as `[role] content` and Cognition sends the string as a single user turn after two system messages. The session keeps a real alternation; the provider never sees it. | `cognition/compaction.py:153`; `cognition/assembler.py:70`; `cognition/service.py:339-340` | Send `session.messages` as messages |
| L3 | high [prop: medium] | undermined | No stable prompt prefix: the per-minute clock is the first line of the protected `task_rules` block, which with the tool notes is the bulk of a 1.4k to 6k-token system prompt, regenerated every think. Four small blocks precede it. | `orchestration/scaffolds.py:638, 690-692` | Stable-first ordering; clock and budget hint in the user turn; measure cache hits |
| L4 | high [prop: medium] | over-engineering | One tool call is ~13 bus messages and ~20 fsync'd appends. The latency cost is small (an fsync'd append measured 0.031 ms); the real cost is trace fragmentation (88k streams) and read-back of the action stream per call. | `session.py::_propose_and_await`; `guardian/service.py`; `execution/service.py` | Per-turn appends; traces per session; drop the read-back once typed args arrive on the message |
| L5 | high | bug | Crash-resume restores the step count but not the context: the resumed model starts blind with fewer steps, because `session.messages` is populated only when a progress note exists and re-grounding is off. | `orchestration/resume.py:117-144` | Resume from the session stream (section 8.1); until then, render the restored steps into the context |
| L6 | high | bug | A chat turn can edit the live checkout, cannot commit, and leaves the edit orphaned "for a next attempt" that never comes. | `profiles.py:59`; `session.py::_continues` | S10 |
| L7 | high [prop: medium] | wrong-design | The chat profile is a 20-step, 72-tool, 16k-output task without task semantics: no verify, no worktree, no resume, a synchronous 420 s wait, on a 12k-token input budget, with a fixed prompt of ~3.2k protected tokens plus a ~2.5k-token tool block. | `orchestration/profiles.py` CHAT; `interface/service.py` | Route by intent to a 10 to 20-tool bundle; chat read-only plus `start_task` |
| L8 | medium [prop: low] | wrong-design | Domain and channel knowledge has leaked into the kernel loop: the TV tool list, three TV and dashboard claim regexes, a pronunciation regex, misheard forms of Sim's name and a voice-only refusal rule, in `session.py`; four guards share one `claim_corrected` flag so only the first firing guard per session corrects. | `session.py:184, 189, 193, 236, 338, 553, 556, 1078-1185` | One generic Stop hook plus Verification's trajectory check (section 8.1) |
| L9 | medium [prop: low] | over-engineering | Consumer groups, claim RPC, leases, heartbeats and a per-second lease scan for one worker in one process. Nearly free at this scale (task streams are 0.4% of the ledger). | `orchestration/worker.py`, `claims.py` | Keep behind the interface; do not extend |
| L10 | medium [corr: low] | undermined | The loop features that matter (re-grounding, parallel read batches, clean revisions, delegation, strong-tier escalation) are built, unit-tested and all off by default; the live config has no `[orchestration]` section. ### 13.9 What the skeptics changed

Of 93 findings judged by two skeptics each (a handful of the last proportionality verdicts were still running when this was written; the findings they cover were verified by hand):

- **None was refuted outright.** The readers' factual claims held against the code in every case.
- **Severity was lowered on 41.** The commonest reason: the cost is disk, audit noise or design debt rather than latency or safety at this scale (the fsync'd append is 0.031 ms; the wake-all ticker is under 1% of the machine; the lease protocol is 0.4% of the ledger).
- **Claims were sharpened on 30.** The important sharpenings are in the tables above: the flattening happens in the compactor, not the assembler; the clock is first in the `task_rules` block, not the whole prompt; the 0.25 s recall budget is not what forces the hashing embedder; `full_suite_ran`'s failure rate is mostly the check working; the direct `tool.run()` sites are six, and the TV one is off by default; the broadcast drop-on-error is the documented bus contract.
- **Two were re-characterised as the project's own "unconnected wire" shape** rather than wrong design (C1, S6), which is the right frame: coherent design, consumers written, producer never wired, nothing fails.

### 13.10 Completeness critic

A final agent was asked what the nine readers missed, looking across their boundaries at data ownership, the identity model, schema versioning, secrets, the v1 relationship, git as runtime state, disk growth, external binaries, packaging hygiene and the stray files in the tree. Its findings were still being produced when this document was written; the items it was pointed at are covered in the tables above where a reader reached them (B7 data ownership, V3 identity, S2 secrets, P5 and W10 v1, B12 git as runtime state, B3 and V11 disk, T11 binaries, and the packaging and stray-file items in section 8.4). Anything it adds beyond those will be appended as section 13.11 in a follow-up commit rather than held back.

## 14. Method, evidence and limits

### 14.1 How this review was produced

The review ran on 2026-09-18 against `main` at `38a9049` in `/Users/saeed/ws/Simorgh`, with the live data directory at `~/.simorgh` read but never written. It was generated by Claude Code using Claude Fable 5.1, in three passes:

1. **Scouting by hand.** The architecture documents, the module map, the previous audit and fact-check, the import graph, the hot path of one chat turn (`interface/service.py` → `orchestration/session.py::_run` → `cognition/service.py` → provider → `_propose_and_await` → Guardian → Execution), the ledger on disk, the live config, the loader's gate, and the test layout. Every number in section 2 was measured in this pass.

2. **A review workflow of 201 agents.** Nine readers, one per concern (substrate; kernel and lifecycle; the agent loop; safety; cognition, memory and growth; surfaces; tools and domains; testing and process; whole-system proportionality), each instructed to read code rather than history, to cite file and line, to run cheap commands for runtime facts, and never to boot the system, run the suite, call a paid model or modify a file. Each of their 93 findings was then attacked by two skeptics with different lenses (factual correctness today; proportionality at this scale), each instructed to default to "refuted" if they could not verify the claim themselves. A completeness critic looked for what the readers missed.

3. **A design workflow of 8 agents.** Four architects wrote complete re-architectures from different lenses (modern harness; cognitive architecture and long-horizon autonomy; production systems and evaluation; embodied household agent). Three judges with different mandates (a maintainer, a researcher, the creator's advocate) scored all four on fit to reality, technical soundness, future alignment, capability gain and safety, and resolved their contradictions. A synthesiser produced one target architecture from the winning spine with the best-scored grafts.

Headline claims in Part I were re-verified by hand before writing: the `tools=` argument ignored by every provider; the flattened transcript at `compaction.py:153` and `service.py:339-340`; the Kernel's auto-approve default at `kernel/service.py:203`; `shell: bool = True` at `execution/config.py:193`; the open camera routes at `httpapi.py:922`; the six direct `tool.run()` sites; `learn.self_patch.applied` published only from `learning/pipeline.py:196` with no publisher of `learn.pipeline.run`; the CHAT profile at 72 tools by importing the module; the Supervisor's `poll_once` having no caller; and 22,849 of 26,737 action streams being `ring_live`.

### 14.2 Commands behind the numbers

```
# size
find simorgh -name '*.py' | xargs wc -l | tail -1          # 86,996
find tests -name 'test_*.py' | wc -l                        # 447
find src -name '*.py' | xargs wc -l | tail -1               # 16,441

# import graph: only kernel imports other subsystems

# ledger

ls ~/.simorgh/ledger/streams | wc -l                         # 118,215
ls ~/.simorgh/ledger/streams | sed 's/%3A.*//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#   88356 trace, 26737 action, 2431 task, 350 verify, 310 reflect
grep -h -o '"tool": *"[a-z_:]*"' ~/.simorgh/ledger/streams/action%3A* | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#   22849 ring_live, 721 cam_stream, 570 run_shell, 473 read_file, 431 search_code ...

# profiles
python3 -c "from simorgh.orchestration import profiles as p; print(len(p.CHAT.tools), len(p.VOICE_CHAT.tools))"   # 72 58

# the open self-improvement loop
grep -rn 'LEARN_SELF_PATCH_APPLIED' simorgh --include='*.py'  # one publisher: learning/pipeline.py:196
grep -rn 'LEARN_PIPELINE_RUN' simorgh --include='*.py'        # subscribed in learning/service.py; published nowhere

# native tool calling

# incident comments
```

### 14.3 The design panel's scores

| Proposal | Judge 1 | Judge 2 | Judge 3 | Total / 150 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harness (modern agent loop) | 40 | 43 | 41 | **124** |
| Cognitive architecture | 39 | 40 | 39 | 118 |
| Production systems and evals | 38 | 42 | 40 | 120 |
| Embodied household agent | 35 | 39 | 36 | 110 |

All three judges named the harness proposal the winner, each with the same three conditions: physical-safety closure and zero-contract wires first; native tools and streaming in the first quarter; the package consolidation last and gated by evals. The disagreements they resolved (where the transcript lives; bus RPC vs in-process injection for the model call; when native tool use lands; the re-grounding trigger; the unit of budget; the shape of the growth loop; tiers vs a physical axis; the telemetry split) are each recorded in the relevant row of section 8.1 with the side chosen and why.

### 14.4 Limits of this review

- **Nothing was run.** No agent booted the system, ran the suite, or called a paid model. Runtime claims come from the ledger, the config and cheap `python -c` imports. Latency figures are the project's own measurements from 2026-09-18.
- **The ledger window is nine days** (2026-09-09 to 2026-09-17) and dominated by dashboard and benchmark traffic, so "never called" for a tool means "not in that window".
- **Severity is a judgment.** Two skeptics per finding reduce but do not remove it. The brackets in the tables show where they disagreed with the reader.
- **The migration estimates are for one developer working through coding agents** and are order-of-magnitude. The order matters; the weeks do not.
- **The panel's view of "where agents are going"** is grounded in patterns that are well established by 2026 (native tool use, typed transcripts, compaction, agent definitions, sub-agents, skills, tiered memory, MCP, eval-driven development). Where an architect cited a specific system or paper, it was checked for confidence and otherwise stated as a pattern. Predictions beyond that are marked as such.
- **This is one more document in a project that already has too many.** Its recommendations should be turned into findings entries and issues, and this file should be frozen once they are.
